opus-5.5.text:
I think there's actually more consensus than people realize, but it's a shallow consensus. If you ask almost anyone in the field, whether they come from the language model side, the vision side, or robotics, they'll agree that intelligence needs some kind of internal model of the world, something that can anticipate what happens next, imagine consequences, and plan. Nobody really argues anymore that pure pattern matching on static data is the endgame.

But once you go one level deeper, the consensus falls apart. What should the brain predict? Pixels, tokens, latent representations, actions? Should prediction happen in the raw sensory space, or in some abstract space where you throw away the irrelevant details? Is next-token prediction on text already a predictive brain, just one that lives in a very compressed, human-curated world? People disagree a lot on these questions, and I think that's where the real research lies.

My own bias, which I've been fairly open about, is that language alone isn't enough. Language is a beautiful but very lossy projection of the world. Humans built it on top of a huge amount of perceptual and physical understanding that we never write down. If you only learn from text, you inherit the conclusions without the grounding. So I believe the predictive brain has to be built substantially from visual and sensory experience, from watching how the world unfolds, interacting with it, and being surprised by it.

There's also a practical disagreement about timing. Some people think you can keep scaling language models and bolt perception on later. Others, including me, think the representation itself has to be learned differently from the start. Otherwise you end up with something that talks about the world fluently but doesn't really model it.

So I'd summarize it this way: everyone agrees we need a predictive brain, but there's no consensus on what it predicts, what it learns from, or how we'd know when we've built one. For a researcher, that's the exciting part. A consensus that's too complete usually means the interesting problems are already gone.

r001.rationale: The response says there is more consensus than people realize, but it does not say consensus has been moving toward agreement over the past year.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the consensus is actually much broader than people realize, but it's a consensus about the destination, not about the road.

If you ask almost anyone serious in the field, whether they come from the LLM world, from robotics, from neuroscience, or from computer vision like me, "does an intelligent system need an internal model that predicts how the world will evolve," they'll say yes. Yann LeCun has been saying this for years with JEPA and world models. Even people building pure language models would agree that next-token prediction is, at some level, learning to predict. Nobody really argues that a system which only reacts, without anticipating, is going to get you to general intelligence. So on that abstract question, I'd say there's near-universal agreement.

Where the consensus completely falls apart is on what "predictive" actually means and what you predict in. Do you predict in pixel space? In a learned latent space? In language? Do you do it via diffusion, via autoregression, via some energy-based objective? That's where the field is genuinely split, and I think it's a healthy split, because honestly none of us know yet.

My own view, coming from vision, is that the language-centric camp has been a little too comfortable. Language is an incredibly compressed, human-curated representation of the world. It's a shortcut. You get a lot of structure for free because humans already did the abstraction. But a child doesn't learn physics by reading about it. They learn by watching things fall, by pushing things, by being surprised. The predictive brain in biology is overwhelmingly a sensory, embodied thing. So when I see progress on video generation models, I don't mainly see them as content tools, I see them as evidence that we're starting to learn predictive structure directly from raw observation. That's the part I think is still underappreciated.

So to answer your question directly: high consensus on "we need it," low consensus on "how," and I'd add a third layer where I think there's actually a quiet disagreement nobody states out loud, which is whether current scaling of language models already is building that predictive brain implicitly, or whether it's a fundamentally different object that needs its own architecture and its own data. I lean toward the second, but I'd be lying if I said that was settled.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad agreement that intelligent systems need prediction, but does not say consensus has been moving toward that view over the past year.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s more consensus around prediction as a principle than around how to implement it. The idea that intelligence needs to anticipate what happens next—to understand how the world changes and what your actions will do—is pretty compelling. But “building a predictive brain” can mean very different things to different people.

What are you predicting? The next token, the next frame, or some abstract representation of a future state? And at what timescale? Those choices matter. Predicting every pixel accurately isn’t necessarily the same as understanding what’s happening.

So I’d say there’s broad agreement on the intuition, but much less agreement on the objective, the representation, or the architecture. And I think the question of whether prediction alone is sufficient for intelligence is still open.

r001.rationale: The response says there is broad agreement on prediction as a principle, but it does not state that consensus has been increasing over the past year.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s broad agreement on the intuition, but much less agreement on what it means in practice. If by a predictive brain you mean a system that learns how the world evolves and can anticipate the consequences of its actions, that’s a very compelling direction. But that doesn’t tell us what we should predict, in which representation, or over what time horizon.

You can predict the next token, the next frame, or a more abstract state of the world. Those are all prediction tasks, but they may encourage very different capabilities. Predicting every pixel, for example, can require modeling details that aren’t relevant to making a decision.

So I would distinguish consensus around prediction as a useful learning principle from consensus around a particular architecture or objective. The first is fairly strong. The second is still an open research question.

r001.rationale: The response says there is broad agreement around prediction as a learning principle, but it does not state that consensus has been increasing over the past year.
